explanation: `H(q) = A` is bare forwarding; `H`'s list binds no `y`, so `A`'s `y` comes from the enclosing parameter `y` of `F`: `F(5)` is `6`.
`H(y) = A` binds its own `y`, which bare forwarding passes to `A`: `H(0)` is `A(0)`, whatever `F`'s `y` is.
A formula inside the closed list `H(q)` lifts `A` and supplies its `y` from the enclosing parameter binding; a closed list gains no parameter, but it can reuse an enclosing one.
A clause branch is closed at its own level; its formula `A + 0` lifts `A` with the enclosing parameter `y` of `F`.
No parameter binding supplies `y` to `A` inside the closed list `H(q)`, so the reference stays a zero-argument demand of `A`, which requires an argument: an arity error at run time.
Bare forwarding supplies `Coll`'s collector from `A`'s own collector `xs` and re-spreads it, so `Coll` counts the two items.
A fixed source binding is passed whole even into a collector: `Coll` collects the one pair `(1, 2)`.
`Cnt(*xs)` accepts an empty supply, so a bare `Cnt` in a formula is never lifted: it is `Cnt`'s cached zero-supply read (`0`), not a forward of `F`'s `xs`.

explanation: A block nested in a clause branch is an ordinary owner with its own Grace: `{ y - ~x }` infers `(x, y)`, so `f(1, 10)` is `10 - 1`.
Bare forwarding reads `count`'s parameter name `collection`; the body binds `collection`, so the row is `count(collection)`.
Inside `H(q)`, `A`'s `y` and `z` come from the nearest enclosing parameter bindings, `F`'s `y` and `G`'s `z`: `3 * 10 + 2 + 1`.
`G(y)` binds its own `y`, the nearest binding of that name, so `A + 0` lifts with `G`'s `y`: `G(7)` is `70`.
The property `y = 4` is not a parameter binding, so it never supplies `A`; `G` gains `y` as a new forwarded parameter, and the carrier `F` forwards its argument to `G`: `F(2)` is `20`.
